content_voiceover: P A X five alt rearranged ALL is another one of the newer WHO-recognized molecular subtypes, and this slide gives you two testable facts. First, the demographics, these patients tend to present at an older age compared to typical childhood ALL, with a median presenting age of fifteen point four years, so this is a subtype you're more likely to see in adolescents and young adults rather than in toddlers. Second, the outcomes data, which actually looks quite good and differs a bit depending on which cooperative group you look at. In the Children's Oncology Group trial A A L L zero two three two, the five-year event-free survival was seventy-one point five percent plus or minus seven percent. In the St. Jude Total sixteen study, the five-year event-free survival was notably higher, at eighty-two point seven percent. The gap between these two numbers is worth noting, it may reflect differences in treatment intensity, risk stratification, or patient population between the two protocols, but the overall message for boards is that P A X five alt is generally considered a favorable to intermediate risk subtype, distinct from the true P A X five P eight zero R point mutation subtype, which behaves differently.
